title: Gaia Alari's Lilting Animations are Drawn Frame by Frame
description: Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elabor
body:
Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elaborate animations put on strikingly tactile performances as fleeting marks of oil pastel and charcoal dance across the screen.
Meandering botanical forms, gestural bodies, and sweeping birds converge into fluid loops that create a rhythm reminiscent of a stream of consciousness. Whether Alari is collaborating with a brand, exploring personal interests, or creating static illustrations, it’s clear that each piece tells a distinct story. Watch more from the artist on Vimeo and keep up with her explorations on Instagram.

title: Three NYC Museum Unions Ratify Contracts, Averting Strikes
description:
News
                Workers at the American Folk Art Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and Guggenheim Museum had bargained for higher pa
body:
News
                Workers at the American Folk Art Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and Guggenheim Museum had bargained for higher pay and better working conditions. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Workers at the American Folk Art Museum rally outside the institution’s annual gala at the Mandarin Oriental in Manhattan on May 6, 2026. (photos Aaron Short/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            After months of collective bargaining and looming strikes, unionized staff at the Brooklyn Museum and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum have ratified their second contracts with their respective institutions, while the American Folk Art Museum (AFAM) union is celebrating the ratification of its first contract with the museum. These developments come after the Whitney Museum of American Art, Brooklyn Museum, and AFAM unions jointly voted to authorize strike action last month if a tentative agreement could not be reached, falling in line with the Guggenheim union, which had voted in favor of a strike at the end of June.However, unionized Whitney staff have set a strike deadline of Monday, October 5, ahead of the press and VIP previews and opening date for the museum's Roy Lichtenstein retrospective that week, which they are prepared to picket throughout. Ahead of their second contracts, the Brooklyn Museum and the Guggenheim were under intense scrutiny early into 2025 after initiating sweeping staff cuts, which they attributed to mounting financial constraints.

title: Maia Ruth Lee Invites Us to Embody the Interval
description:
Pocket Review
                The works draw on motifs of migration, but the motifs themselves migrate across the gallery.
body:
Pocket Review
                The works draw on motifs of migration, but the motifs themselves migrate across the gallery.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            detail of "B.B. Tetris 1-4" (2026)(photo Min Park/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Translation never arrives in Maia Ruth Lee’s solo exhibition at Tina Kim Gallery, Double Vision. Instead, it is a condition to be embodied and probed. Much like her parents — Bible translators who moved to Nepal and developed a written alphabet for the oral Sherpa language — Lee unfolds the act of translation in her new show.Grid-like patterning inspired by the luggage at Kathmandu airport, illegible glyphs, and images from the family archive act as a recurring visual language across canvas, latex, and steel. The works draw on motifs of migration, but the motifs themselves migrate across the gallery, mutating as they take on new forms. Stacking, for instance, evokes playfulness in the modular canvases of the B.B. Tetris series (all 2026) and heaviness in “Expandable Luggage” (2026), where the growing height perhaps suggests a belabored migration. Here, translation acts as a migration of a kind: some things carry across while others are left behind.Installation view of Maia Ruth Lee's "Double Vision Video work #1" (2026) (photo Min Park/Hyperallergic).

title: Mamdani Doubles Grants for NYC Artists
description:
News
                For the last 20 years, city-funded grants for individual artists have remained at $5,000.
body:
News
                For the last 20 years, city-funded grants for individual artists have remained at $5,000.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Culture Commissioner Diya Vij annoucing increased city grants for artists in a video on Instagram (via Instagram) 
    
        
            Individual artists can now receive up to $10,000 in city-funded grants, double the amount of previous appropriations, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs (DCLA) announced today, October 2. DCLA annually disperses these grants across the city to local partners, which then administer funds to cultural organizations, arts nonprofits, and artists. The previous baseline of $5,000 has remained in place for nearly 20 years, according to the Mayor’s Office. “Artists are forced to make hard choices when it comes to living in this city and getting paid,” Mamdani said in an Instagram announcement where he paints at an easel across from DCLA Commissioner Diya Vij. “There’s never been a better time to apply. Anyone who's an artist in our city and has a vision is welcome to.” With the exception of Staten Island, which opens applications in November, all other boroughs are currently accepting applications. The Bronx Council on the Arts accepts grants until October 30; the Brooklyn Arts Council until October 11; the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council until November 12; and the New York Foundation for the Arts in Queens until November 17. The news comes three months after Mamdani struck an agreement with the City Council to distribute $323.8 million for the DCLA as part of the Fiscal Year 2027 budget, the city government’s highest-ever yearly appropriation. He has also supported arts organizations by giving a portion of $8.4 million in small business grants to public art commissions and arts programming. “Artists are the beating heart of this city, but it’s not always easy to make a living as one,” Vij added in the video. One of the murals from the pair “Superhero Responds” (2021) at the L train 1 Avenue stop (photo Valentina Di Liscia/Hyperallergic)According to a recent Cultured magazine report, artists in New York City are often forced to buttress their creative work with other income streams, such as full-time day jobs, sex work, or teaching gigs. A January report from the Center for an Urban Future also noted that the city’s resident artist population has fallen 4.4% since 2019, its first measurable decline in decades, and evidence of the city’s lack of affordable housing and income stability for artists. To further curb these costs, DCLA’s Materials for the Arts (MFTA) program will officially begin its new monthly shopping program for artist grantees on October 19. Held on the second Monday of each month, grantees can book an appointment to take free materials from the MFTA’s 35,000-square-foot warehouse, which receives millions of pounds worth of arts donations each year. Earlier on in Mamdani’s tenure, writer Aruna D’Souza probed the longstanding affordability crisis for artists in an essay for Hyperallergic, but remained optimistic that Mamdani’s administration would address those issues. “We do need more affordable artist studios. We do need more affordable housing, period. We do need more support for artists, and more possibilities for artist-run spaces and galleries,” D’Souza wrote. “But we also have glimmers of hope: a new mayor, a new culture czar, and — as far as I can see from the artists I talk to — a new determination not to let New York’s culture scene wither away.

title: Francis Lee Rogers, Painter and Avid Birdwatcher, Found Dead in Central Park
description:
News
                The 63-year-old artist, who was unhoused, was known as the “Grandma Moses of Central Park” for her various
body:
News
                The 63-year-old artist, who was unhoused, was known as the “Grandma Moses of Central Park” for her various depictions of its fauna and flora. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Francis Lee Rogers holds up one of her paintings (photo via Facebook)Francis Lee Rogers, a 63-year-old artist whose neighbors and subjects were the birds of Central Park, died on Sunday, September 27. Law enforcement sources told the New York Post that Rogers, who was unhoused, had been found beaten to death under the gazebo she called home, though the New York Police Department could not confirm the individual's identity to Hyperallergic due to the ongoing investigation. Rogers had become a fixture in the park as an avid birdwatcher and painter of its various locations, particularly in the Ramble, the heavily wooded section she frequented most often. "We used to call her the Grandma Moses of Central Park," Robert "Birding Bob" DeCandido told Hyperallergic in a phone interview, comparing the artist to the renowned folk landscape painter. "But she probably wouldn't want all this sympathy. She didn't call attention to herself."The artist reached Central Park through a difficult path, having gone by multiple names throughout her life. She was known as Elise Bainbridge Hill when she was the subject of Karen Gehres's 2007 documentary Begging Naked, in which she recounted running away from home as a teen, surviving as a sex worker, persevering through a heroin addiction, and finding space for her art in between.

title: Mala Iqbal Paints the Space We Share With Strangers
description:
Art Review
                Her new paintings remind us that the world is a room we share with strangers, most of whom are lookin
body:
Art Review
                Her new paintings remind us that the world is a room we share with strangers, most of whom are looking elsewhere. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Mala Iqbal’s “Subway Riders” (2026) by the front windows of JJ Murphy gallery on Manhattan's Lower East Side (all photos Hrag Vartanian/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Figures jostle the surface of every Mala Iqbal canvas with the energy of a great metropolis. Many are bathed in an orange and yellow glow, a tinge of artifice for people who live under electric light, places where even the sun isn't enough. Some of the paintings forgo that effect, like "Through the Curtains” (2026). Left to right, we see a scene of collapse, which is obscured by a tulle curtain rendering like a faded negative; a figure reacts, almost numbly; and ultimately another curtain finishes the scene with a pictograph-like pattern — life, transformed by a screen, experienced by someone, and turned into an indecipherable language. I view it as a metaphor for how our screens deliver collapse and violence with every scroll, faster than we can process it.Mala Iqbal, “Through the Curtains” (2026)Each work is about the construction of reality, sometimes cobbled together, other times layered and occasionally philosophized through the arrangement of images, figures, and signs. Social realism casts a long shadow, though the mood is closer to Matisse's ease. Her “Times Square” (2026) has the chalky palette of Ben Shahn, which gives the image its own terroir, and it never sours into despair.Many of the paintings take place in subways, places where false intimacies give us the illusion of knowing. But the artist never drops the urban masks we wear as we stare into faces that look away or are obstructed and rendered into shapely flourishes, bringing to light strange but enticing surfaces. One figure is recognizable, that of the painter’s partner, artist Angela Dufresne, in “Subway Riders” (2026), who herself seems to be recording something of her own, staring towards us but not at us, reminding us how our own relationships depict us as much as we depict them.Detail of Mala Iqbal, “Transparent Friend” (2025)

title: Queer Artists Say Tom of Finland Foundation Has Lost Its Way
description:
Feature
                Former artist residents of the LA nonprofit fear leadership has strayed from the radical, queer energy t
body:
Feature
                Former artist residents of the LA nonprofit fear leadership has strayed from the radical, queer energy that Tom and his house embody.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Tom of Finland birthday celebration at TOM House, 2017 (photo courtesy Ruben Esparza)
    
        
            LOS ANGELES — For over four decades, the Tom of Finland Foundation has been a vital hub for queer artists. Now, an acrimonious rift between the foundation’s board and its co-founder leaves its future uncertain.The nonprofit foundation was established in 1984 to preserve the art and legacy of Tom of Finland (born Touko Laaksonen, 1920–1991), whose erotic depictions of hypermasculine men — sailors, lumberjacks, and leather-clad bikers — have become iconic images of queer culture. Over the years, its scope grew beyond Tom’s work. The foundation began supporting contemporary artists through exhibitions and acquisitions, and in 2011, it started an artist residency program based out of its headquarters, an Echo Park craftsman home known affectionately as “TOM House.” On Monday, September 28, a group of 41 former artist residents released an open letter to the foundation’s board in which they expressed concern over “the lack of transparency and abrupt interruption of several programs by the current administration,” specifically the Artist-in-Residence (AIR) program, which they say was “discontinued without prior communication or warning.” They also claim that “nearly the entire staff” of the House was laid off this past June. The letter asks the board to “guarantee the continuation of the Foundation’s mission, not only by preserving the legacy of Tom of Finland and his work, but also by maintaining an active commitment to new generations of queer and erotic artists through a residency program, mentorship, support, exhibitions, research, and access to the Foundation’s unique archive.” Carta Monir at the Tom of Finland House (photo Mark Hanauer, courtesy Carta Monir)Carta Monir, a 2022 AIR and coordinator of the open letter, told Hyperallergic that the board was “refusing to answer any questions.” “It felt vital to write the letter,” Monir said. “It’s clear that, unless there’s public scrutiny, they won’t be transparent.”
